questions.title: Checked Exception Definition
questions.description: What is a checked exception in Java?
options: An exception that is checked by the JVM at runtime
An exception that the compiler forces you to handle or declare (IOException, SQLException)
An exception that is automatically handled by the default handler
An exception that only occurs during compilation
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions are exceptions that the Java compiler forces you to either catch (try-catch) or declare in the method signature (throws). Examples include IOException, SQLException, and ClassNotFoundException. If you do not handle or declare them, the code will not compile.
hints: The compiler 'checks' whether you have handled these exceptions
RuntimeException and its subclasses are NOT checked

questions.title: Unchecked Exception
questions.description: Which of the following is an unchecked exception in Java?
questions.explanation: NullPointerException is an unchecked exception because it extends RuntimeException, which is a subclass of Exception. Unchecked exceptions do not need to be declared or caught. IOException, FileNotFoundException, and SQLException are all checked exceptions that must be handled or declared.
hints: Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException
They are typically programming errors that could have been avoided

questions.title: Try-Catch Syntax
questions.description: What is the correct syntax for a try-catch block in Java?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax is 'try { } catch (ExceptionType variableName) { }'. The catch block must specify the exception type as a parameter in parentheses. The 'then' keyword is not used in Java exception handling. Multiple catch blocks can be chained for different exception types.
hints: The exception type and variable are enclosed in parentheses
There is no 'then' keyword in Java exception handling

questions.title: Finally Block
questions.description: When does the 'finally' block in a try-catch-finally structure execute?
options: Only if no exception is thrown
Only if an exception is thrown
Always, regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught
Only if the exception is caught
questions.explanation: The finally block always executes, regardless of whether an exception is thrown, caught, or neither. It executes even if there is a return statement in the try or catch block. The finally block is typically used for cleanup operations like closing files, releasing network connections, or freeing resources.
hints: This block is guaranteed to run under all circumstances
It is typically used for cleanup operations

questions.title: Throws Keyword
questions.description: What does the 'throws' keyword in a method signature indicate?
options: The method will definitely throw that exception
The method might throw the specified exception(s) and callers must handle or declare them
The method throws away the exception silently
The exception can be ignored by any caller
questions.explanation: The 'throws' keyword in a method signature declares that the method might throw the specified exception(s). It does not mean the exception will be thrown — only that the method could potentially throw it. Callers of the method must either catch these exceptions or declare them in their own throws clause.
hints: This keyword is part of the method declaration, not a statement
Think of it as a warning to callers: 'be prepared for this exception'

questions.title: Throw Keyword vs Throws
questions.description: What is the difference between 'throw' and 'throws' in Java?
options: throw is used to throw an exception from code; throws declares possible exceptions in a method signature
throw is used in method signatures; throws is used in code blocks
There is no difference — they are interchangeable
throw is for checked exceptions; throws is for unchecked exceptions
questions.explanation: throw (without s) is a statement that actually throws an exception object from code: throw new IOException(). throws (with s) is part of the method signature that declares which exceptions the method might throw. throw can only throw one exception at a time; throws can list multiple exception types separated by commas.
hints: One is an action (execution), the other is a declaration (compiler)
One is a statement inside the method body, the other is in the method signature

questions.title: Multiple Catch Blocks
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
options: Index Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
questions.explanation: arr[5] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException because the array has only 3 elements (indices 0-2). This exception is caught by the first catch block (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException), which is more specific than the general Exception catch block. The getMessage() method returns detail information about the exception: 'Index 5 out of bounds for length 3'. When an exception is caught, only the first matching catch block executes.
hints: Catch blocks are checked in order — the first matching one catches the exception
More specific exceptions should be caught before more general ones

questions.title: Exception Propagation
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
questions.explanation: Execution: main calls methodA() which prints 'A ', then calls methodB() which prints 'B '. methodB then throws an ArithmeticException. The exception propagates up: methodB has no handler, so it goes to methodA. methodA has no handler either, so it propagates to main, where the try-catch catches it (prints 'Caught '). The lines 'A2' in methodA and anything after methodA() call in main never execute. Finally 'Done' is printed. This is called exception propagation — the exception moves up the call stack until caught.
hints: When an exception is thrown, execution jumps to the nearest matching catch block
Statements after the exception source do not execute

questions.title: Custom Exception
questions.description: Which of the following correctly defines a custom checked exception in Java?
questions.explanation: To create a custom checked exception, extend the Exception class. To create a custom unchecked exception, extend RuntimeException. Option A creates an unchecked exception. Option C is invalid because Exception is a class, not an interface. Option D creates a plain class that is not an exception type and cannot be thrown.
hints: Checked exceptions extend Exception directly
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException

questions.title: Try-with-Resources
questions.description: What is the advantage of try-with-resources introduced in Java 7?
options: It allows multiple resources to be tried in sequence
It automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable, even if an exception occurs
It replaces the need for the catch block entirely
questions.explanation: Try-with-resources (try (Resource r = new Resource()) { ... }) automatically closes any resource that implements AutoCloseable or Closeable when the try block exits, whether normally or via an exception. This eliminates the need for explicit finally blocks for resource cleanup and prevents resource leaks. Multiple resources can be declared and will be closed in reverse order.
hints: This feature eliminates the need for explicit finally blocks for cleanup
Resources must implement AutoCloseable

questions.title: Multi-catch Exception
questions.description: Which syntax correctly catches multiple exception types in a single catch block (Java 7+)?
questions.explanation: Multi-catch uses the pipe symbol '|' to separate exception types in a single catch block: catch (IOException | SQLException e). This reduces code duplication when multiple exceptions should be handled identically. The exceptions in a multi-catch must not be in a parent-child relationship. Option B uses || (logical OR), which is incorrect. Option C uses comma (not valid). Option D uses & (bitwise AND), which is incorrect.
hints: The pipe symbol separates exception types in multi-catch
The exceptions must be unrelated (not in the same inheritance hierarchy)

questions.title: FileReader Basic Usage
questions.description: Which classes are commonly used together to read text files efficiently in Java?
questions.explanation: FileReader reads character files, and BufferedReader wraps it to provide efficient reading (buffering) and convenient methods like readLine(). The pattern is: BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader('file.txt')). This is the standard way to read text files in Java.
hints: One class reads raw characters from a file; the other adds buffering and line-by-line reading
readLine() is a key method for reading text files

questions.title: FileWriter and PrintWriter
questions.description: Which is the recommended way to write formatted text to a file in Java?
options: PrintWriter with print(), println(), and printf() methods
questions.explanation: PrintWriter provides convenient print(), println(), and printf() methods for writing formatted text to a file, similar to System.out. The typical pattern is: PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter('file.txt')). PrintWriter's format methods are more convenient than BufferedWriter's write() method for most text writing needs.
hints: This class provides the same convenient methods as System.out
It supports printf-style formatting

questions.title: File Reading with Scanner
questions.description: Which of the following correctly opens a file for reading with Scanner?
questions.explanation: To read from a file with Scanner, pass a File object to the Scanner constructor: new Scanner(new File('data.txt')). The String constructor of Scanner reads from a String, not a file. Scanner can also read from InputStream, Path, and Readable sources. Scanner provides convenient methods like next(), nextInt(), nextLine(), and hasNext() for parsing.
hints: Scanner does not have a constructor that takes a file path as a String
You need to create a File object first

questions.title: File I/O with Try-With-Resources
questions.description: Which version correctly reads a file and automatically closes resources?
options: Version A: uses try-with-resources and automatically closes the reader
Version B: correctly handles file reading with no resource leak risk
Version C: incorrectly uses finally instead of catch for closing
questions.explanation: Version A uses try-with-resources, which automatically closes the BufferedReader (and underlying FileReader) when the try block exits, even if an exception occurs. Version B has a resource leak — if readLine() throws an exception, the reader is never closed. Version C has a potential bug: if br is null, br.close() will throw a NullPointerException, and the variable is also not accessible in the finally block if declared inside try. Try-with-resources is the safest and cleanest approach.
hints: Version A declares the resource in the try parentheses
Resources declared in try-with-resources are automatically closed

questions.title: Exception Hierarchy—Error vs Exception
questions.description: In the Java exception hierarchy, what is the difference between Error and Exception?
options: Error is checked, Exception is unchecked
Error represents serious system problems (OutOfMemoryError) that should not be caught; Exception represents conditions a program might catch
Error is for input/output problems; Exception is for logic errors
Error and Exception are the same thing
questions.explanation: Both Error and Exception extend Throwable. Error represents serious system-level problems (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, VirtualMachineError) that a program should not try to catch — they indicate the JVM is in a state from which recovery is unlikely. Exception represents conditions that a well-written program might reasonably catch and handle. Errors are unchecked (subclasses of Error are not required to be caught/declared), but they are not meant to be caught.
hints: Think of Error as 'JVM-level catastrophe' and Exception as 'application-level problem'
You should NOT try to catch Errors in normal code

questions.title: Finally with Return
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
questions.explanation: When both try and finally have return statements, the finally return overrides the try return. Before returning 1, the finally block executes and returns 3. The return value from try (1) is discarded. This is a dangerous pattern — it is generally recommended not to use return in finally blocks as it can suppress exceptions and cause unexpected behavior. The code compiles but may not do what was intended.
hints: The finally block always executes, even if there is a return in try
A return in finally overrides any previous return value

questions.title: Suppressed Exceptions
questions.description: What happens if both the try block and the implicit close() in try-with-resources throw exceptions?
options: Only the try exception is thrown; the close() exception is ignored
The try exception is thrown, and the close() exception is added as a suppressed exception
Only the close() exception is thrown
questions.explanation: When using try-with-resources, if both the try block and the close() method throw exceptions, the exception from the try block is the one that propagates, and the close() exception is added to it as a 'suppressed' exception. You can retrieve suppressed exceptions using Throwable.getSuppressed(). This is better than the old try-finally pattern where the close() exception would completely hide the try exception.
hints: The primary exception 'wins' and the secondary exception is attached to it
Use getSuppressed() to retrieve the hidden exception

questions.title: Try-With-Resources Multiple Resources
questions.description: What is the correct way to declare multiple resources in a single try-with-resources statement?
options: C: resources are declared inside the try block body
questions.explanation: Multiple resources in try-with-resources are separated by semicolons (not commas). Each resource declaration is a complete statement. Resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration (pw closed first, then br). All resources must implement AutoCloseable. Declaring resources inside the try body (Option C) would not use try-with-resources automatic closing.
hints: Resources are declared with semicolons, similar to variable declarations
The close order is the reverse of the declaration order

questions.title: Reading All Lines from a File
questions.description: Which Java 8+ method reads all lines from a file into a List<String> in one call?
questions.explanation: Files.readAllLines(Path) reads all lines from a file into a List<String>. It is a convenient utility method in java.nio.file.Files introduced in Java 8. Files.readString() (Java 11) reads the entire file content as a single String. For large files, Files.lines() returns a Stream<String> that can be processed lazily without loading everything into memory.
hints: This method is in the java.nio.file.Files class
It returns a List<String> where each element is one line
